Fund

Fund in stages. Release money at gates that pass on evidence, not on dates.

  1. 01How much should we fund?Tool

    Fund the data and the harness first, then the agents.

    A board that funds agents first and data second pays twice.

    Release money in four stages. Each gate passes on a scorecard reading, not on a delivery date.

    Size every stage in cost per completed outcome, not in licences or agent counts.

    Decide this

    • The budget for the first 13 months, split by layer: data, harness, agents and change.
    • The scorecard criteria that release each next tranche.
    • Who signs each gate. Usually the CFO with the program sponsor.
    • The baseline cost per completed outcome for each candidate workflow.

    Metric to watch

    Cost per completed outcome against baseline, per workflow, read at every gate.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Cost per completed outcome
    • Framework: The 30-month plan
    • Blueprints

    Try it · Funding calculator · illustrative numbers

  2. 02How do we build the business case?

    Compare agents, people and vendors on one basis: cost per completed outcome.

    A cheap action that leaves a person to finish the job is not cheap.

    Count delay too. Faster decisions, fewer penalties and released cash often outweigh hours saved.

    Never promise a chain level above its weakest handoff.

    Decide this

    • The baseline per workflow: volume, cycle time, touches and cost per completed outcome.
    • The value levers you will book: hours, speed, cash and penalties avoided.
    • The level each step can reach under the ceiling rules.
    • The weakest handoff in each chain, and the cost to fix it.

    Metric to watch

    Value booked against value planned, at each gate.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Cost per completed outcome
    • Framework: The weakest-link rule
    • Reference architecture
  3. 03How do we know it is working?

    Read value and risk together, every month, for each agent family.

    The value signal must rise faster than the risk counterweight.

    A red counterweight holds promotion for the whole family.

    Report outcomes, not activity. The number of agents is not a result.

    Decide this

    • One value signal per agent family, such as days to resolve or cost per completed outcome.
    • One risk counterweight per family, such as reversal rate or audit findings.
    • The drag to remove, and the drag to keep on purpose.
    • The monthly forum that reads the scorecard and acts on it.

    Metric to watch

    Value signal trend against risk signal trend, per agent family.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: The value–risk flywheel
    • Framework: Cost per completed outcome
    • Blueprints

Prioritize

Pick decisions that are frequent, small and reversible. Fix the weakest link first.

  1. 04What should we fund first?Tool

    Fund the unit that moves: a decision inside a task, not a whole process.

    Start where decisions are frequent, small and reversible, and where data passes its quality gate.

    Score each candidate on value, feasibility and its autonomy ceiling.

    Fund the weakest link before the agent.

    Decide this

    • A long list of candidate decision steps, written as decisions.
    • A value, feasibility and ceiling score for each step.
    • Wave 1: two or three steps that can reach L3 within a year.
    • The handoffs and data fixes that must come first.

    Metric to watch

    Share of the portfolio budget on steps with a ceiling of L3 or higher.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Materiality and reversibility
    • Framework: The weakest-link rule
    • Blueprints

    Try it · What-to-fund prioritizer · illustrative numbers

  2. 05What should we never automate?

    Deciding where not to automate is a control, not a matter of taste.

    Keep a person deciding when the judgment is the product, the error is irreversible, or the law reserves it.

    A capable agent at L2 beside a person is often the higher-value design.

    Review the list like any other control.

    Decide this

    • The do-not-automate list, with a named owner.
    • The review cycle for the list. At least once a year.
    • Where agents still help on listed work: investigate, draft, match and monitor.
    • Who may add or remove an item.

    Metric to watch

    Agent actions on listed steps. The target is zero.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: When not to automate
    • Controls library
  3. 06Build, buy or partner?

    Own what lasts: controls, context, definitions, skills and decision traces.

    Treat models as replaceable parts behind a model gateway.

    Buy commodity tools where the contract lets you keep the traces and switch.

    Partner for speed, but keep accountability with your own executives.

    Decide this

    • Which harness parts you own and run yourself.
    • Exit terms: export of traces, instructions, evaluation sets and data.
    • The model gateway that lets you switch models without rework.
    • The internal owner for each partner-run component.

    Metric to watch

    Time and cost to switch one model or one tool, tested once a year.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: The ten-part harness
    • Framework: Human-led, agent-operated
    • Reference architecture

Govern

Govern the change with named owners, clear decision rights and separated duties.

  1. 07How do we govern the change?Tool

    Govern with a charter, an agent register and gates.

    Every agent has a named owner with the authority to stop it.

    A small council sets policy. Process owners run their agents.

    Promotion needs evidence and a human gate. Demotion happens by rule.

    Decide this

    • The ten-line charter, signed by the CEO.
    • The governance council: members, cadence and decision rights.
    • The agent register and its lifecycle states.
    • The RACI for promotion, limits, releases and the kill switch.

    Metric to watch

    Share of running agents with a named owner, a current register entry and a passed gate. The target is all of them.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Human-led, agent-operated
    • Framework: Earned on evidence, taken back by rule
    • Controls library
    • Self-improving loops: govern how agents change

    Try it · Governance RACI generator · illustrative numbers

  2. 08Who is accountable when an agent gets it wrong?

    A named executive is accountable, never a model or a vendor.

    Each agent acts on behalf of an accountable person, who can stop it.

    The person who approves an agent’s actions may not change its limits, instructions or tools.

    Every human override becomes a labelled error the program learns from.

    Decide this

    • The accountable owner for each agent family.
    • The delegation chain written into each agent identity.
    • The separation between approvers and the people who change limits.
    • How overrides reach the team that improves the agent.

    Metric to watch

    Segregation-of-duties conflicts found in access reviews. The target is zero.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: The ten-part harness
    • Framework: Earned on evidence, taken back by rule
    • Controls library
  3. 09How do we manage risk, regulators and auditors?

    Bring internal audit in at design, not at go-live.

    Map your controls to public frameworks, such as the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act.

    Every action leaves a trace: who acted, for whom, under which policy, with what evidence.

    If the trace fails, the action fails.

    Decide this

    • Which steps are high-risk uses or key financial controls. These stay at L2 until legal and audit approve more.
    • The evidence pack an auditor gets for any single action.
    • The control library and its owner.
    • How incidents and findings reach the board.

    Metric to watch

    Open audit findings on agent steps, and the days to close them.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Materiality and reversibility
    • Framework: The ten-part harness
    • Controls library

People

Build the roles that run agents. Move people to the hard cases.

  1. 10What is our hire and upskill plan?Tool

    Five roles run the agent-operated enterprise: agent owner, harness engineer, evaluation engineer, process redesigner and AI risk lead.

    Fill most of them from inside. Your process experts know the exceptions.

    Hire where no internal path exists. That is usually harness and evaluation skill.

    Decide this

    • The definition of each role and where it reports.
    • Headcount for each role at 12 and 24 months.
    • Reskilling paths for affected teams, with time to proficiency.
    • The share you fill from inside, and the share you hire.

    Metric to watch

    Roles filled against plan, and the share filled from inside.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Six-dimension maturity
    • Framework: The 30-month plan

    Try it · Hire-and-upskill planner · illustrative numbers

  2. 11How do we redesign roles and the operating model?

    The agent removes the investigation, not the person.

    Agents investigate, match, draft and monitor. Deterministic engines compute and post.

    Named people sign, release money and decide about safety and about people.

    Redesign the work around that split first. Then change the org chart.

    Decide this

    • The new split of work for each process, step by step.
    • Which roles become exception handlers, approvers or agent owners.
    • The span of control for people who supervise agents.
    • What a central team owns, and what process owners own.

    Metric to watch

    Share of human time on exceptions and judgment, against routine work.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: When not to automate
    • Framework: Propose, validate, route, commit
    • Blueprints
  3. 12How do we bring people with us?

    Say plainly what changes and what stays human.

    Human hours can rise slightly from L2 to L3, because the escalations are the hardest cases.

    The value comes from speed and better use of people, not only hours saved.

    Treat every override as a lesson, not a failure.

    Decide this

    • The message to affected teams, before pilots start.
    • Training for approvers: what a good decision card shows.
    • How override reasons reach the agent team.
    • Your commitments on redeployment.

    Metric to watch

    Override rate with reason codes, and approver time per decision card.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: The autonomy scale, L0 to L5
    • Framework: Earned on evidence, taken back by rule

Trust

Trust a step, not an agent. Earn each level on evidence; lose it by rule.

  1. 13How far can we trust an agent?Tool

    Trust a step, not an agent. Each step earns its level on evidence and passes a human gate.

    The book’s illustrative bar for L2 to L3: at least 95% approved without edits over 1,000 or more actions.

    That run lasts three months, includes a quarter-end, and keeps reversals below 0.5%.

    Promotion is never automatic.

    Decide this

    • The target level for each step, under its ceiling.
    • The exit criteria for each level.
    • Who signs each promotion.
    • The demotion triggers that act automatically.

    Metric to watch

    Approval-without-edit rate and reversal rate, per step.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Earned on evidence, taken back by rule
    • Framework: The autonomy scale, L0 to L5
    • Controls library

    Try it · Trust ladder · illustrative numbers

  2. 14When may an agent act without a person?Tool

    Only when the expected gain beats the expected loss.

    Let G be the gain when the action is right, and L the loss when it is wrong.

    The agent may act alone when its confidence is at least L ÷ (G + L).

    Bigger stakes raise the bar automatically.

    Decide this

    • The gain and loss estimates for each step, signed by the process owner.
    • The confidence measure, and how you calibrate it.
    • The route when confidence falls short: a decision card to a person.
    • How often you recalibrate.

    Metric to watch

    Calibration: stated confidence against observed accuracy.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Propose, validate, route, commit
    • See one decision run

    Try it · Decision threshold check · illustrative numbers

Control

Keep limits outside the model. Read the whole fleet on one page each week.

  1. 15How do we stay in control?Tool

    Put limits outside the model, where the agent cannot change them.

    Read the whole fleet on one page every week.

    Test the kill switch every quarter.

    Be able to stop one agent, one scope or the whole fleet in minutes.

    Decide this

    • The weekly control-room view, and who reads it.
    • Limits per step: amount, risk score, counterparty class and confidence.
    • Operating envelopes: deadlines, call budgets, retries and loop guards.
    • Kill switch owners and the test schedule.
    • Which agent changes are one-way doors, and who approves them.

    Metric to watch

    Days since the last kill switch test, and exceptions handled within service level.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: The ten-part harness
    • Framework: The value–risk flywheel
    • Controls library
    • Reference architecture
    • Decision trace viewer
    • Self-improving loops

    Try it · Weekly control room · illustrative numbers

  2. 16What happens when something goes wrong?

    The step drops a level by rule.

    Triggers include an error above threshold, a failed data gate, a process or model change, or an audit finding.

    Work routes to people with full context.

    The decision trace shows what the agent saw, decided and did.

    Decide this

    • Demotion triggers and thresholds for each step.
    • The incident path: who is called, and in what order.
    • How you find and reverse affected actions.
    • The evidence needed before the step is promoted again.

    Metric to watch

    Time to detect and time to contain an agent incident.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Earned on evidence, taken back by rule
    • Framework: The ten-part harness
    • Controls library

Scale

Scale on the weakest dimension, not the average. Reuse the harness every time.

  1. 17How do we scale from pilot to portfolio?

    Scale on the weakest maturity dimension, not the average.

    Reuse the harness, the evaluation sets and the agent contract.

    Retire interfaces rather than rebuild them.

    A stage-four claim with no reuse and many open pilots is a stage-three company with more agents.

    Decide this

    • Your score on the six maturity dimensions, with evidence.
    • The reuse rule: no new agent outside the shared harness.
    • Which open pilots to stop.
    • The handoffs to upgrade so that chains can rise.

    Metric to watch

    Reuse rate of harness components, and pilots closed or scaled.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: Six-dimension maturity
    • Framework: The weakest-link rule
    • Blueprints
    • Reference architecture
  2. 18How fast can we move?

    The book’s reference plan runs about 30 months, with a gate at the end of each phase.

    Mobilize in three months. Build foundations and pilots by month 13.

    Go live in a first region by month 19. Scale through month 30.

    Start with a 100-day plan, not a five-year vision.

    Decide this

    • The first 100 days: charter, team, baselines and the first shadow agents.
    • The phase gates and their scorecard criteria.
    • What you decommission as you go.
    • The handover to the line organization.

    Metric to watch

    Gates passed on scorecard readings, not only on milestones.

    Go deeper

    • Framework: The 30-month plan
    • Framework: Six-dimension maturity
